name: Semantic Embeddings
question: Which texts mean the same thing?
summary: An embedding model maps text to a dense vector, typically a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, so that texts with similar meaning land close together. Search becomes a nearest-neighbour lookup by cosine similarity, which matches paraphrases and synonyms that share no words at all.
useCases: Users describe things in their own words, not your terminology
Question answering over documentation or knowledge bases

items.detail: split documents into passages, ~200–800 tokens, with overlap
query and document embedded separately, compared fast
compare on MTEB, then on your own queries

steps: Chunk documents on natural boundaries such as headings and paragraphs, with a little overlap
Embed chunks with the same model you will use for queries
Store vectors with metadata: source, section, date, permissions
Measure recall@k on real questions before tuning anything else
pitfalls: Weak on exact terms: IDs, codes, rare names
Domain jargon may need a domain-tuned model
Changing models means re-embedding the whole corpus

comparison.best: Misses exact IDs and rare terms

steps.title: Chunk the documents
steps.text: Split each document into passages of about 200 words with a 40-word overlap, so no idea is cut at a boundary. One help article becomes three chunks.

steps.title: Embed every chunk
steps.text: The model turns each chunk into 384 numbers. Normalizing each vector to unit length lets a plain dot product act as cosine similarity.

steps.title: Embed the query with the same model
steps.text: The question goes through the same model. A vector from a different model lives in a different space and can’t be compared.

steps.title: Score by cosine similarity
steps.text: Compare the query vector with every chunk vector. The refunds chunk scores 0.71 even though it shares no words with the question.

steps.title: Return the nearest neighbours
steps.text: Sort by score and keep the top k. With k = 2 the two refund chunks come back; the shipping chunk at 0.22 does not.

steps.title: Measure recall@k
steps.text: Run 200 real questions with known answers and count how often the right chunk is in the top 5. Tune chunking and the model against this number.

pros: Matches meaning, so paraphrases and synonyms are found
One model covers questions, clustering, deduplication and recommendations
Fast at query time: documents are embedded once, ahead of time
Many strong open and hosted models, compared on MTEB
cons: Weak on exact tokens such as error codes, SKUs and IDs
Similarity scores are hard to explain to users
Domain jargon may be blurred by a general model
Switching models means re-embedding the whole corpus
avoidWhen: Queries are mostly exact codes or names (use BM25, or hybrid)
You need an auditable reason why each result matched

playgroundGuide.scenario: A payments app’s help centre has eight articles. A customer types a question in their own words, the question and every article are embedded with the same model, and the articles are ranked by cosine similarity. Your job is to return every relevant article and nothing else.
controls: Pick the customer’s question, including a bare error code.
Set k, the number of results, and a minimum similarity below which results are dropped.
Tick the box to embed the query with a different model than the documents.

outputs.name: Recall@k
outputs.meaning: Relevant articles returned ÷ all relevant articles. Did we find everything?

outputs.name: Precision@k
outputs.meaning: Relevant articles returned ÷ articles returned. How much noise came with it?

outputs.name: Results returned
outputs.meaning: How many articles survive both the top-k cut and the similarity threshold.

outputs.name: Top result relevant
outputs.meaning: Whether the very first result is one of the right articles.

goals: Compute cosine similarity and explain why normalized vectors make it a dot product
Explain recall@k and precision@k and how k and a threshold trade them off
Explain why queries and documents must be embedded with the same model

practice.scenario: On an investment app's help centre, a user types “why did money leave my account on the 5th?”. Semantic search matches it to the article “Auto-debit for SIP instalments”, even though the two share almost no words.

industries.use: Help-centre search in customers’ own words
Match job descriptions to résumés by meaning
Find similar clinical notes or trial eligibility criteria

practice.analogy: A good librarian who hears “books about sad robots” and walks you to the right shelf, even though no title says that.

library.name: sentence-transformers
library.what: The standard open-source library for embeddings: thousands of pretrained models, CPU-friendly, one line to encode.

samples.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")     # 384 dims, runs on CPU
docs = ["Auto-debit for SIP instalments",
        "How to change your registered mobile number",
        "Brokerage charges for intraday trades"]
doc_vecs = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)

query = model.encode("why did money leave my account on the 5th?",
                     normalize_embeddings=True)
scores = util.cos_sim(query, doc_vecs)[0]
for s, d in sorted(zip(scores.tolist(), docs), reverse=True):
    print(f"{s:.2f}  {d}")

numericDrill.question: Compute the cosine similarity of a = [1, 2, 2] and b = [2, 1, 2].
numericDrill.answer: a · b = 2 + 2 + 4 = 8. ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 3. Cosine = 8 ÷ 9 ≈ 0.889: very similar direction.

interview.question: What's the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
interview.answer: A bi-encoder embeds query and document separately, so document vectors are precomputed and search is fast. A cross-encoder reads them together for more accurate relevance but can't precompute, so it's used to re-rank a short list.

interview.question: How do you choose a chunk size?
interview.answer: Big enough to hold a complete idea, small enough to be specific: often 200–800 tokens with some overlap, split on headings or paragraphs. Tune it by measuring recall@k on real questions.

mistakes.mistake: Embedding queries and documents with different models
mistakes.fix: Use the same model, including any required query/document prefixes

mistakes.mistake: Fixed-size chunks that cut sentences and tables
mistakes.fix: Chunk on structure: headings, paragraphs, table boundaries

quiz.question: Customers search “money deducted twice”. The right article is titled “Duplicate debit reversal”, and keyword search finds nothing. What helps most?
quiz.explanation: The query and title share no words but mean the same thing. Dense embeddings match meaning.

quiz.question: Two symptom notes embed as a = [3, 4] and b = [4, 3]. What is their cosine similarity?
Product search quality is poor after launch. Which of these could be causing it? Select all that apply.
options: Documents were embedded with one model and queries with another
Chunks cut specification tables in half
Cosine similarity is computed on normalized vectors
Most queries are bare SKU codes
quiz.explanation: Mismatched models, broken chunks and code-only queries all hurt dense search. Cosine on normalized vectors is correct.

quiz.question: The team switched embedding models for new policy documents only; old documents keep their old vectors. What happens to searches over old documents?
options: They improve, because queries use the better model
Scores against old vectors become meaningless
Nothing changes while the dimensions match
Only the similarity threshold needs lowering
quiz.explanation: Different models produce unrelated vector spaces. Re-embed the whole corpus when you change models.

quiz.question: On 200 test questions, the right chunk appears in the top 5 for 168 of them. What is recall@5?
Why is a bi-encoder, not a cross-encoder, used to search 10 million help-centre chunks?
options: Document vectors can be computed once, ahead of time
quiz.explanation: A bi-encoder embeds documents independently, so search is a fast vector comparison. A cross-encoder must read every query–document pair.

quiz.question: A firm embeds each 12,000-word contract as a single vector, and clause questions retrieve the wrong contracts. What is the best fix?
options: Chunk on clause and section boundaries with a little overlap
Use a larger embedding model on whole contracts
quiz.explanation: One vector for a whole contract blurs every clause together. Chunks of a few hundred tokens keep each clause findable.

quiz.question: What should you store next to each chunk vector in the index? Select all that apply.
options: The float values again as a text string
quiz.explanation: Metadata lets you cite, filter by date or course, and enforce permissions. Duplicating the vector as text adds nothing.

quiz.question: Both vectors are normalized to unit length and their dot product is 0.83. What is their cosine similarity?
quiz.explanation: For unit vectors cosine = a · b ÷ (1 × 1), so it equals the dot product.

quiz.question: 5 million chunks are embedded at 768 float32 dimensions. How much memory do the raw vectors need?
quiz.explanation: 768 × 4 B = 3,072 B per vector × 5 million ≈ 15.4 GB.

quiz.question: Passengers write to support in Hindi, Tamil and English. How should you choose the embedding model?
options: Pick the model with the most dimensions
Shortlist multilingual models and compare recall on real queries in each language
Translate everything to English and use any model
quiz.explanation: Language coverage varies by model. Measure on your own queries, per language.

quiz.question: After switching models, a similarity threshold of 0.8 that worked before now returns almost nothing. Why?
options: Score ranges differ between models, so thresholds must be re-tuned
The index needs rebuilding with more shards
quiz.explanation: Each model spreads its scores differently. Tune thresholds per model on your own data, or rely on ranking.

quiz.question: A hospital is choosing an embedding model for clinical guideline search. Which steps are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Build a labelled set of real clinician questions
Compare recall@k of each candidate on that set
Pick the model with the largest vectors
quiz.explanation: Public benchmarks shortlist; your own labelled questions decide. Vector size alone says little about quality.

quiz.question: Exact nearest-neighbour search over 200 million vectors takes seconds per query. What is the standard remedy?
options: An approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW
quiz.explanation: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders-of-magnitude faster search.

quiz.question: The team uses an E5 model but embeds queries and products with no prefixes, and quality is lower than published results. What is the likely fix?
options: Add the “query: ” and “passage: ” prefixes the model was trained with
quiz.explanation: E5 models expect these prefixes. Follow the model card’s input format.

quiz.question: Besides search, what else can the same claim-description embeddings do well?
options: Flag near-duplicate claims by very high cosine similarity
quiz.explanation: Embeddings support clustering, deduplication and recommendations, not arithmetic or OCR.

quiz.question: Why add a 40-word overlap between consecutive 200-word chunks?
options: So an idea split at a boundary still appears whole in one chunk
To make every chunk the same vector
quiz.explanation: Overlap reduces the chance that the sentence answering a question is cut in half.

quiz.question: Which queries are likely to fail with dense-only search? Select all that apply.
options: “my internet is really slow at night”
quiz.explanation: Reference numbers and IMEIs are exact tokens with little meaning. Natural-language questions suit dense search.

quiz.question: What is the cosine similarity of a = [1, 0, 1] and b = [0, 1, 1]?
A résumé-search index holds 1 million embedded chunks, and 5,000 new résumés arrive daily. The model is unchanged. What should you do?
options: Embed only the new résumés with the same model and add them
Re-embed all 1 million chunks every day
Embed new résumés with the newest model available
quiz.explanation: Re-embedding everything is needed only when the model changes. New content just needs the same model.
